title: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])
hookLine: God stoops down to lift the poor from the dust

cards: Right now, somewhere on earth, the sun is rising. Somewhere else it's setting. At every moment, someone is waking up and someone is going to bed.
A short psalm turns that fact into praise that never stops, a relay around the planet. And then, halfway through, it looks down from the sky, all the way down to the garbage heap at the edge of town.

teach.b: Psalm 112 in the Douay, 113 in most Bibles. It opens: "Praise the Lord, ye children: praise ye the name of the Lord."
Children follows the Latin, pueri, a word that can also mean servants, and the Hebrew does say servants: you who serve the Lord.
Then the sun: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise." East to west, morning to night.
Then it climbs as high as it can go: God is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens. Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high? And then the surprise.

teach.h: OUT OF THE DUNGHILL, TO PRINCES.
teach.b: This God looks down on the low things in heaven and in earth, and the psalm keeps going down: "Raising up the needy from the earth, and lifting up the poor out of the dunghill: That he may place him with princes, with the princes of his people."
The dunghill was probably the town refuse heap, often explained as the place where the poorest people slept and begged.
The God above the heavens stoops all the way to the dump and seats someone from there at the royal table. One more: the barren woman is given a home, the joyful mother of children.
Hannah sings nearly the same lines about the poor and the dunghill when her son is born, and Mary sings the same turning-over of the world in the Magnificat.
This psalm begins the Hallel, the psalms of praise sung at Passover. Some readers think these were the hymn Jesus and his friends sang at the Last Supper before going out to the Mount of Olives.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 112 [113] at Evening Prayer on some Sundays and on feasts, and hear it at Mass; in Latin it is known as Laudate pueri, and composers have set it for Vespers.

games.q: the psalm has just called God high above the heavens. where does it go next?
o: all the way down, lifting the poor from the dunghill to sit with princes.
to the king's palace, to praise the king.
games.why: raising up the needy from the earth, and lifting up the poor out of the dunghill, that he may place him with princes. the higher God is, the lower he stoops.

practice: Bring to mind one person who's low right now: discouraged, overlooked, stuck on their own small dunghill.
Think of one small thing that might lift them a little: a message, a call, a true compliment, a coffee, an invitation to sit at your table.
If you pray, pray for them in the psalm's words, raising up the needy; if you don't, simply hold them in mind and choose your one small thing.

wordCard.voice: Laudate pueri. Latin for praise, O servants, the psalm's name at Vespers, praise running around the world all day, to the God who stoops to lift the poor. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: praise, O servants (or children), the psalm's first words and its name at Vespers.
